vt35_inti_and_the_andes.topic: Inti, the Coricancha, Inti Raymi, the Punchao, Taki Onqoy and the sun in Andean Christianity

claims.text: Coricancha in Cusco was dedicated to Inti; its walls were covered in sheets of gold; in 1533, when the Spanish demanded a gold ransom for Atahualpa, most of the gold was collected from the Coricancha

The Dominicans built the church and convent of Santo Domingo on the site; construction took most of a century; the present building dates from after the 1650 earthquake; four rooms of the Inca temple survive within the convent

Inti Raymi was the Inca new-year festival of the sun at the June solstice, credited to Pachacuti; the last held with the Inca ruler present is dated to 1535 in popular accounts; Garcilaso de la Vega described it
Viceroy Francisco de Toledo in 1572 prohibited ceremonies associated with the Inca cult, Inti Raymi among them (Infobae 2026)
Revived in 1944 as a theatrical reconstruction by Humberto Vidal Unda and Faustino Espinoza Navarro, based largely on Garcilaso; staged at Sacsayhuamán on 24 June
Dean (Duke 1999): Corpus Christi in colonial Cuzco marked 'the triumph of Christian orthodoxy over the imperial Inka patron (the Sun)'
Smarthistory: Corpus Christi coincided with the Inka solstice celebration of Inti Raymi; Cusco Corpus Christi series of 18 canvases, 16 survive

Taki Onqoy arose in the 1560s around Huamanga; Luis de Olvera claimed in 1577 he discovered and corrected it in 1564; leaders said revived huacas would defeat the God of the Christians and send illness to the Spaniards

Cristóbal de Albornoz led the suppression; penalties included public shaming, shaving, whipping, forced labour, exile; women confined in convents; kurakas fined; leaders taken to Cusco to renounce; Olvera claimed destroying 700 huacas and over 8,000 idols
Varón and Guibovich argue Albornoz exaggerated the movement's spread in his 1570 probanza; it was local to parts of Ayacucho, Huancavelica, Apurímac

Toledo ordered the attack on Vilcabamba; Túpac Amaru captured 1572 and executed in Cusco 24 September 1572; clerics pleaded for him; Philip II disapproved; the Spanish seized the Punchao, a gold image holding the hearts of dead Inca kings

Julien 2002: Toledo took the Punchao to Spain in 1581; after his death in 1582 the Council of the Indies seized items; a gold idol appears in the inventory after Philip II's death in 1598, possibly kept in Madrid's Casa del Tesoro into the early 1600s; Wikipedia says the sacred items were destroyed
The Willaq Umu were the high priests of the Sun, usually brothers of the Sapa Inca; Villac Umu joined Almagro's 1535 Chile expedition and defected back to Cusco to aid the uprising

UNESCO 2011: Qoyllurit'i pilgrimage combines Catholicism and worship of pre-Hispanic nature deities; begins 58 days after Easter; about a hundred dances; procession to Tayancani to greet the first rays of sunlight
